raw: {"slots": {"question": [{"claim": "The paper asks whether regional political climate moderates the link between individual political conservatism and COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and uptake. It notes that earlier work examined orientation and climate separately but not how they interact.", "quotes": [{"text": "While previous research has identified the unique impact of both political orientation and political climate on vaccination attitudes, there has been little research on the interaction between personal political orientation and local political climate.", "page": 2}, {"text": "The present research examines political climate as a potential moderator of the association between political orientation and COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and uptake.", "page": 2}]}], "central_claim": [{"claim": "Political climate, measured by regional 2020 presidential vote, is more strongly linked to vaccine and booster hesitancy for more conservative individuals than for liberal ones. Conservatives living in liberal regions are more likely to get boosted.", "quotes": [{"text": "our findings indicate that political climate, as represented through regional 2020 presidential election votes, has a stronger association with vaccine and booster hesitancy for individuals who are higher on political conservatism as compared to those who are politically liberal.", "page": 8}, {"text": "By looking at political orientation and region climate, we identify a novel and important finding, specifically that conservative individuals are more likely to received booster doses in liberal regions.", "page": 10}]}], "evidence": [{"claim": "The data come from a cross-sectional online self-report survey of a nonprobability convenience sample of 683 US participants, collected in March–April 2023 through Qualtrics Panels. The sample was quota-recruited as half White and half Black.", "quotes": [{"text": "We collected online survey data from 683 participants between March 8 and April 19, 2023.", "page": 1}, {"text": "This was an online self-reported study in which a nonprobability convenience sample was recruited from the United States between March 8 and April 19, 2023.", "page": 2}, {"text": "Half of the sample was requested to be White (and no other racial identity), and half the sample was requested to be Black (and no other racial identity).", "page": 4}]}, {"claim": "Regional climate is measured as the percent Republican vote in the 2020 election, matched to each participant's zip code. Hesitancy and vaccination status are modeled with linear and logistic regressions that include a conservatism × climate interaction term and demographic controls.", "quotes": [{"text": "We assessed regional political climate using zip code data provided by participants and 2020 presidential election results sourced from the New York Times [22].", "page": 3}, {"text": "Multiple linear regression models were built to assess the association between political conservatism and conservative regional climate with vaccine hesitancy, controlling for age, gender, education, income, race, and perceived vaccine access.", "page": 4}]}], "key_findings": [{"claim": "Individual conservatism and a conservative regional climate are each associated with higher vaccine and booster hesitancy and with lower self-reported vaccination and boosting.", "quotes": [{"text": "Political conservatism and conservative regional climate were both associated with higher levels of COVID-19 vaccine and booster hesitancy and lower rates of self-reported vaccination and boosting, when controlling for age, education, income, and race.", "page": 10}]}, {"claim": "Hesitancy rises with conservatism, and the rise is steeper for people living in more conservative regions. Liberals show low hesitancy regardless of their region.", "quotes": [{"text": "As political conservatism increases vaccine hesitancy also increases, but this increase is even greater for individuals who live in a more conservative regional climate.", "page": 10}]}, {"claim": "For booster status, the most conservative participants in liberal climates had roughly a 60% likelihood of being boosted. Conservatives in conservative climates had a likelihood under 35%.", "quotes": [{"text": "The most conservative participants in liberal climates were 60% likely to get boosted, while conservatives in conservative climates were less than 35% likely to get boosted (OR =.83, p = .026).", "page": 8}]}, {"claim": "The interaction was not significant for initial vaccination status.
